x: # Welcome, friend We're glad you're here. This site is a free gift from our church family to yours. It's for anyone who wants to know why Christians believe Jesus lived, died, and rose again, and how to share that hope gently. ## What this site is A place to explore the evidence for Jesus at your own pace. We make the case as strongly as the facts allow, and we tell you honestly where scholars still disagree. We would rather you trust us than be impressed by us. ## How to use it - **Have a question?** Type it in the "Ask a question" box. It will point you to an answer we have checked. - **Heard a hard objection?** Open "Answer an objection." Each card gives a 30-second answer, the evidence, and where to read more. - **Want the heart of it?** Read "The resurrection." Everything rests there (1 Corinthians 15:14). - **Want to grow?** Try "Learn mode," with short lessons and a quiz. - **Talking with a friend of another faith?** "What others say" explains their view fairly and how to respond kindly. ## A word on how we speak "But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect," (1 Peter 3:15, BSB) Answers matter. So does kindness. Win the person, not just the argument. ## Where our material comes from Bible quotes come from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB), which is free to share. Books and articles by scholars are summarized in our own words and linked. Our research began with a public dossier by 0xSero, which we link to with thanks: https://github.com/0xSero/all-historical-evidence-of-jesus-christ

## You are welcome here Doubt is not the opposite of faith. Thomas doubted, and Jesus did not send him away. He met him: "Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe." (John 20:27, BSB) A father once said to Jesus, "I do believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24, BSB), and Jesus helped him. You can bring honest questions too. ## A simple way to begin 1. **Name your question.** Write down the one thing that bothers you most. Then look for it under "Answer an objection" or type it into "Ask a question." 2. **Start with the center.** The Christian claim stands or falls on one event, the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3-8). Read the resurrection page first. 3. **Read a Gospel yourself.** Mark is short and can be read in one sitting. John wrote his Gospel "so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name." (John 20:31, BSB) 4. **Talk to someone.** Questions are easier with a friend, a pastor or a church small group. 5. **Be honest with God.** You can pray even while you are unsure. Jesus said, "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest." (Matthew 11:28, BSB) ## Talking with a friend about faith Peter tells believers how to speak about their hope: > "But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience, so that those who slander you may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ." (1 Peter 3:15-16, BSB) Paul adds: > "Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone." (Colossians 4:6, BSB) **If you are the one sharing:** - **Listen first.** Ask what they believe and why, and let them finish. - **Ask questions.** "What would change your mind?" often helps more than a long argument. - **Be gentle and respectful.** You are talking with a person, not winning a debate. - **Be honest.** If you don't know an answer, say so, and offer to look into it together. - **Admit what is debated.** Each answer card has a "Still debated" note. Use it. - **Live it.** Peter ties our words to "good behavior in Christ." People notice how we treat them. - **Keep Jesus at the center.** Side questions matter, but the main question is who Jesus is and whether He rose. - **Leave room.** You don't have to settle everything in one conversation. Pray for your friend and stay their friend. **If you are the one asking:** it is fair to ask hard questions, and it is fair to ask Christians to show their work. That is what this site tries to do. ## An invitation When Nathanael doubted, Philip didn't argue. He invited him: "'Can anything good come from Nazareth?' Nathanael asked. 'Come and see,' said Philip." (John 1:46, BSB) That is our invitation too.

x: > Note: Only the relevant section is reproduced. Bracketed editorial insertions are from the translator. 1. As to His works severally, and His cures effected upon body and soul, and the mysteries of His doctrine, and the resurrection from the dead, these have been most authoritatively set forth by His disciples and apostles before us. On the whole world there pressed a most fearful darkness; and the rocks were rent by an earthquake, and many places in Judea and other districts were thrown down. This darkness Thallus, in the third book of his History, calls, as appears to me without reason, an eclipse of the sun. For the Hebrews celebrate the passover on the 14th day according to the moon, and the passion of our Saviour fails on the day before the passover; but an eclipse of the sun takes place only when the moon comes under the sun. And it cannot happen at any other time but in the interval between the first day of the new moon and the last of the old, that is, at their junction: how then should an eclipse be supposed to happen when the moon is almost diametrically opposite the sun? Let that opinion pass however; let it carry the majority with it; and let this portent of the world be deemed an eclipse of the sun, like others a portent only to the eye. Phlegon records that, in the time of Tiberius Caesar, at full moon, there was a full eclipse of the sun from the sixth hour to the ninth — manifestly that one of which we speak. But what has an eclipse in common with an earthquake, the rending rocks, and the resurrection of the dead, and so great a perturbation throughout the universe? Surely no such event as this is recorded for a long period. But it was a darkness induced by God, because the Lord happened then to suffer. And calculation makes out that the period of 70 weeks, as noted in Daniel, is completed at this time.

t: The Spirit of the Lord is on Me
x: Isaiah 61:1-2 In his hometown synagogue, Jesus reads this passage and announces, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.' t: A voice crying in the wilderness
x: Isaiah 40:3 Isaiah hears a voice calling for a road to be prepared for the LORD. All four Gospels apply it to John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Jesus. x: Psalm 118:22-23 Jesus applies this to himself after the parable of the tenants: the leaders reject him, but God makes him the cornerstone. s: Jesus applies this to himself after the parable of the tenants: the leaders reject him, but God makes him the cornerstone. Peter repeats it before the council after the resurrection.

Some later rabbinic texts also apply it to the Messiah (for example the Talmud, Sukkah 52a, applies it to the Messiah son of David). Resurrection and exaltation
s: The psalm speaks of the LORD's anointed king (mashiach) whom the nations oppose and God declares his son. Paul applies it to the resurrection, Hebrews to Jesus' superiority to angels, and the voice at Jesus' baptism echoes it.

x: Psalm 41:9 David grieves that a trusted friend who shared his bread turned against him. Jesus applies the verse to Judas at the Last Supper. Jewish readers see a lament about a real betrayal in David's life, often linked with Ahithophel. Ministry and passion week

x: Isaiah 50:6 In the third Servant Song the servant does not resist beating, spitting and insult, and trusts God to vindicate him. The Gospels record Jesus struck and spat on during his trial. Jewish readers see the prophet describing his own mistreatment, or Israel's, while trusting God. Suffering and death

x: Jesus was executed by crucifixion under Pontius Pilate. Christian and non-Christian sources agree, and almost no scholar doubts it. Every Gospel ends with the cross, Paul's early creed begins with it (1 Corinthians 15:3), and the Roman historian Tacitus says Christus was executed under Pilate in the reign of Tiberius (Annals 15.44). Habermas lists the death by crucifixion as the first of his Minimal Facts, the short list that needs near-unanimous scholarly agreement. Michael Licona, working through the evidence at length, puts it in his 'historical bedrock' with two other facts, as Habermas reports. This fact matters for the tester because any theory that says Jesus did not really die has to overturn it.
s: Jesus was executed by crucifixion under Pontius Pilate. Christian and non-Christian sources agree, and almost no scholar doubts it.

t: The disciples had experiences they believed were appearances of the risen Jesus
x: Soon after his death, his followers had experiences they took to be meetings with Jesus alive. Even skeptical scholars grant they believed this. The creed Paul passes on lists appearances to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred at once, James and all the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:5-7). The Gospels and Acts tell of individual and group appearances. Habermas counts this as a core Minimal Fact, and Licona places it in the historical bedrock. The fact is about what the disciples experienced and believed, not yet about what caused it. That is why skeptics such as Gerd Lüdemann accept it and then offer hallucination as the cause (see the theory tester).
s: Soon after his death, his followers had experiences they took to be meetings with Jesus alive. Even skeptical scholars grant they believed this.

t: Paul, a persecutor of the church, was turned around by what he believed was an appearance of Jesus
x: Saul of Tarsus tried to destroy the church, then became its best-known missionary, saying the risen Jesus appeared to him. Paul writes in his own letters that he persecuted the church and then received a revelation of Jesus (Galatians 1:13-16), and he puts himself last in the list of appearances (1 Corinthians 15:8-9). Acts tells the story three times, starting in Acts 9. Habermas lists this among his Minimal Facts, and Licona's bedrock includes it. Paul is important for the tester because he was an enemy, not a grieving follower, so theories built on grief or wishful thinking struggle to explain him.
s: Saul of Tarsus tried to destroy the church, then became its best-known missionary, saying the risen Jesus appeared to him.

t: James, the skeptical brother of Jesus, became a leader of the Jerusalem church
x: Jesus' brother James did not believe in him during his ministry, yet later led the church in Jerusalem. Paul says Jesus appeared to him. John 7:5 says his brothers did not believe in him, and Mark 3:21 has his family trying to take charge of him. Paul says the risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7) and later met him as a leader in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19). Josephus records his execution (Antiquities 20.200). Habermas says he goes back and forth on whether to count this as a Minimal Fact (2012, p. 25); Licona treats it as a strong 'second-order' fact because fewer scholars discuss it, not because many deny it (Habermas 2012, pp. 22-23). We label it Confirmed for the facts of the texts and note this nuance on the card.
s: Jesus' brother James did not believe in him during his ministry, yet later led the church in Jerusalem. Paul says Jesus appeared to him.

t: The resurrection was proclaimed very early
x: The claim that Jesus was raised did not grow up decades later. Paul passes on a creed he had already received. In 1 Corinthians 15:3 Paul says he delivered what he had received: that Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day and appeared to named witnesses. Habermas says that for years he folded this early date into the appearances fact, then began to count it as a separate Minimal Fact, because few conclusions are better accepted across the scholarly spectrum (2012, pp. 24-25). Surveying the literature, Habermas reports that 'the vast majority of critical scholars who answer the question place Paul's reception of this material in the mid-30s A.D.' (2005, web copy). Paul likely received it on his visit to Peter and James (Galatians 1:18-19). Even the skeptic Gerd Lüdemann dates the appearance traditions to 'the time between 30 and 33 CE', as quoted by Habermas (Dialog 2006).
s: The claim that Jesus was raised did not grow up decades later. Paul passes on a creed he had already received.

x: The tomb was found empty on the Sunday. A fairly strong majority of scholars accept this, but it is not near-unanimous. Mark 16:1-8 tells of women finding the tomb empty, and Matthew 28:11-15 says the authorities claimed the disciples stole the body, which assumes the body was missing. He is explicit that he has never counted it as a Minimal Fact, because it lacks near-unanimity (2012, p. 25). Craig, by contrast, lists it among his four facts.
s: The tomb was found empty on the Sunday. A fairly strong majority of scholars accept this, but it is not near-unanimous.

t: The resurrection was the centre of the earliest Christian message
x: The first Christians did not treat the resurrection as a side doctrine. It was the heart of what they preached. Paul calls the creed 'of first importance' (1 Corinthians 15:3) and says that if Christ is not raised, faith is useless (15:14, 17). Peter's first sermon in Acts 2 centres on it. Habermas has a few times counted this as a Minimal Fact, but he says himself the case is not quite as strong as for the early date (2012, p. 25), and Licona does not list it. We mark it Contested so the tester does not weigh it.
s: The first Christians did not treat the resurrection as a side doctrine. It was the heart of what they preached.

t: Jesus was buried in a tomb by Joseph of Arimathea
x: All four Gospels say a member of the Jewish council, Joseph of Arimathea, put Jesus in a tomb. Craig counts this as his first fact. Mark 15:42-46 and the other Gospels name Joseph of Arimathea as the man who buried Jesus, and the creed says simply that he was buried (1 Corinthians 15:4). Craig makes the burial the first of the four facts he argues 'any adequate historical hypothesis must account for' (Reasonable Faith article; also his opening statement against Ehrman in 2006). It is not on Habermas's Minimal Facts list, so we mark it Contested: it is argued for by many scholars but not near-unanimous.
s: All four Gospels say a member of the Jewish council, Joseph of Arimathea, put Jesus in a tomb. Craig counts this as his first fact.

t: Women were the first to find the tomb empty
x: Every Gospel says women found the tomb empty. Habermas reports Licona treats female eyewitness testimony as an important issue. Mark 16:1-8, Matthew 28:1-10, Luke 24:1-10 and John 20:1-2 all put women first at the tomb. Apologists argue that a story invented to persuade would not have chosen witnesses whose testimony carried less weight in that culture; Habermas notes Licona gives this question a full treatment (2012, p. 21, citing Licona pp. 349-55). The argument itself is our framing, and the fact depends on the empty tomb, which is Contested, so this record is Contested.
s: Every Gospel says women found the tomb empty. Habermas reports Licona treats female eyewitness testimony as an important issue.

t: The disciples were changed and willing to suffer for their claim
x: The first witnesses went from hiding to public preaching and accepted danger for it. Not every apostle's martyrdom is well attested. Acts 2 shows Peter preaching publicly in Jerusalem weeks after the crucifixion. The site's honest note already says that only some apostles are well attested as martyrs (Peter, James son of Zebedee, James the brother of Jesus), and points to Sean McDowell's grading of each. The point is sincerity: people rarely suffer for something they know is false. It does not show their belief was true, and we mark it Contested at the level of individual apostles.
s: The first witnesses went from hiding to public preaching and accepted danger for it. Not every apostle's martyrdom is well attested.

x: The disciples took the body and lied that he rose. This is the oldest alternative: Matthew 28:11-15 says it was already being told. Habermas notes Hermann Reimarus revived it in the 18th century (CRJ 2001). It explains an empty tomb, but not why the disciples sincerely believed they had seen Jesus, nor why Paul the persecutor and James the skeptic came to believe. Our verdicts are argued judgments.
s: The disciples took the body and lied that he rose.

x: Jesus fainted on the cross, revived in the tomb and was taken for risen. Habermas notes Friedrich Schleiermacher favored this view and that David Strauss is usually thought to have crushed it, so that few scholars supported it after his critique (CRJ 2001). It runs straight into the best attested fact, the death by crucifixion. Even if a man survived, a half-dead figure would inspire pity, not belief that he had conquered death.
s: Jesus fainted on the cross, revived in the tomb and was taken for risen.

x: Grieving followers had private hallucinations of Jesus. Strauss popularized this in the 19th century, and in recent decades Gerd Lüdemann and Jack Kent have argued versions of it (Habermas, CRJ 2001). It takes the appearance experiences seriously, which is its strength. But hallucinations leave the body in the tomb, and Paul was not a grieving follower. Habermas quotes psychologist Gary Collins that hallucinations are individual events that a group cannot share.
s: Grieving followers had private hallucinations of Jesus.

x: The groups who said they saw Jesus shared one hallucination or caught each other's excitement. Lüdemann describes a 'chain reaction' spreading from Peter to the others, including the 500 (as summarized by Habermas, CRJ 2001). Habermas answers that most psychologists treat hallucinations as private; that the examples offered for collective hallucinations involve crowds who expected and wanted to see something; and that the disciples were in fear and grief, not expectation.
s: The groups who said they saw Jesus shared one hallucination or caught each other's excitement.

x: Paul's vision came from guilt or psychological conflict, not from Jesus. Kent proposes that Paul experienced a conversion disorder, while the disciples had grief hallucinations; Habermas sets out and critiques this combination (CRJ 2001). Combining two theories to cover different witnesses multiplies the assumptions, and it still leaves the tomb untouched.
s: Paul's vision came from guilt or psychological conflict, not from Jesus.

t: The story is a legend that grew over time
x: The resurrection story grew slowly from a simpler memory into a miracle tale. Otto Pfleiderer and others thought legend could explain much of the data, though Habermas notes Pfleiderer himself admitted it could not explain it all (CRJ 2001). The main problem is time: the creed in 1 Corinthians 15 shows the claim of appearances to named people was already being passed on very early, before legend had time to grow.
s: The resurrection story grew slowly from a simpler memory into a miracle tale.

t: The women went to the wrong tomb
x: The women got lost, found an empty tomb that was not his, and the story spread. If the women went to the wrong tomb, the authorities or Joseph of Arimathea could have pointed to the right one. The theory is aimed only at the empty tomb, which is itself Contested, so in the tester it touches none of the Confirmed facts. We have not yet opened a primary source for its proponents, so none are named.
s: The women got lost, found an empty tomb that was not his, and the story spread.

t: A twin or impostor was seen
x: Someone who looked like Jesus, perhaps a twin, was mistaken for him. No early source mentions a twin or look-alike. The theory needs an unknown person, an unknown motive, and a deception that fooled close friends, a hostile Pharisee and a skeptical brother. We have not opened a scholarly source naming a proponent, so none is named.
s: Someone who looked like Jesus, perhaps a twin, was mistaken for him.

t: God raised Jesus from the dead
x: Jesus really rose. This is the explanation the first witnesses gave. Craig argues that this hypothesis passes the six tests historian C. Behan McCullagh lists for the best explanation: explanatory scope, explanatory power, plausibility, not ad hoc, in accord with accepted beliefs, and outstripping its rivals (Craig, Reasonable Faith article, citing McCullagh 1984 p. 19). Its cost is that it requires openness to God acting. That is a worldview question the reader has to weigh.
s: Jesus really rose. This is the explanation the first witnesses gave.

x: Exhibit 1: the man is dead. Roman and Christian sources agree Jesus was crucified.
s: Exhibit 1: the man is dead.

x: Exhibit 2: a known tomb, found empty, by women. Presented as contested evidence, with Habermas's 75/25 split shown.
s: Exhibit 2: a known tomb, found empty, by women.

x: Exhibit 3: named witnesses, individuals and groups. The creed's list of witnesses.
s: Exhibit 3: named witnesses, individuals and groups.

x: Exhibit 4: a hostile witness, the church's enemy. Paul in his own words.
s: Exhibit 4: a hostile witness, the church's enemy.

x: Exhibit 5: the brother who did not believe. James, from doubter to leader.
s: Exhibit 5: the brother who did not believe.

x: Exhibit 6: the testimony is early. The creed predates Paul's letter.
s: Exhibit 6: the testimony is early.

x: Exhibit 7: they staked their lives on it. Shown with the honest note that martyrdom evidence varies by apostle.
s: Exhibit 7: they staked their lives on it.

x: Closing: which explanation fits all the exhibits? Uses Craig's McCullagh tests as the jury instruction, with Luckhoo's standard of proof shown on his bio card.
s: Closing: which explanation fits all the exhibits?

x: Allison thinks the tomb was probably empty and that Mary Magdalene and Peter really believed they saw Jesus. He says history alone cannot prove God raised him. Allison is one of the most careful living specialists on the resurrection. In a 2022 interview he said the case for an empty tomb is stronger than the case against it, though not certain, and that early followers, probably first Mary Magdalene and then Peter, believed they saw Jesus after his death. He also holds that these facts do not by themselves force the Christian conclusion, and he finds Paul's brief mention of the 500 too thin to test. He is useful because he grants key facts without being an apologist.
s: Allison thinks the tomb was probably empty and that Mary Magdalene and Peter really believed they saw Jesus. He says history alone cannot prove God raised him.

x: Ehrman grants the crucifixion and that followers, Paul included, had visions of Jesus. He doubts the burial and the empty tomb and says a miracle is never the historian's best answer. In the 2006 Holy Cross debate Ehrman granted that Jesus was crucified and that believers, including Paul, had what he called visions of Jesus. He argued that we cannot know whether Joseph of Arimathea buried Jesus or whether the tomb was empty, and that a miracle can never be the most probable historical explanation. Craig cited Ehrman's earlier Teaching Company lectures as granting the burial and empty tomb; Ehrman said in the debate that he does not agree with that reading, so we show only what he said in the debate.
s: Ehrman grants the crucifixion and that followers, Paul included, had visions of Jesus. He doubts the burial and the empty tomb and says a miracle is never the historian's best answer.

x: Lüdemann agrees Peter had a real experience of seeing Jesus. He calls it a grief vision and says the body stayed dead. Lüdemann is the leading voice for the hallucination or vision theory. t: Isaiah 53 is about the people of Israel, not Jesus.
x: The servant of Isaiah 53 is Jesus. Read the chapter closely and the servant is one person, not the nation. In Isaiah everyone confesses sin, the prophet included, but the servant alone is sinless. He is punished 'for the transgression of My people' (BSB), so he is someone other than the people. He is the one true Israel who brings Israel back to God. He gives his life as a guilt offering for others, dies and is buried with a rich man, and then lives again and sees his offspring. Only Jesus fits every line, and the New Testament says so plainly. Many early Jewish sources, such as the Targum and the Talmud, connect the passage with the Messiah. The 'servant is Israel' reading is old too (Origen met it around AD 248), but it became the majority Jewish view only after Rashi in the Middle Ages. Only the servant is sinless. In Isaiah everyone confesses sin, the prophet too: 'Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips' (Isaiah 6:5), and 'We all like sheep have gone astray' and the LORD laid on the servant 'the iniquity of us all' (Isaiah 53:6). But of the servant alone it says 'He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth' (Isaiah 53:9, BSB). He suffers for the people, so he is not the people. Isaiah 53:8 says 'He was stricken for the transgression of My people' (BSB). The prophet's people are Israel, and the servant is punished on their behalf. He is the one true Israel, who restores Israel. Isaiah 49:3 does call this servant 'Israel'. Yet two verses later the LORD formed him 'to bring Jacob back to Him' and 'to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the protected ones of Israel' (Isaiah 49:5-6, BSB). Christians answer that the servant is the faithful Israelite who embodies the nation and brings it back, so he is an individual distinct from the nation he restores. He takes our place willingly. 'the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all' (Isaiah 53:6), 'He did not open His mouth' (53:7), and 'His soul is made a guilt offering' (53:10). This is one innocent person carrying the guilt of many, as a sacrifice. He dies and then lives. He is 'cut off from the land of the living' and given 'a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death' (53:8-9), yet afterward 'He will see His offspring, He will prolong His days' and 'will see the light of life' (53:10-11). That is death followed by resurrection. Jesus was crucified between criminals, and then 'there came a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph' who 'placed it in his own new tomb that he had cut into the rock' (Matthew 27:57-60, BSB).
